title: Marlborough
description: Sunny days, cold nights and stony soils at the top of the South Island: the home of a world-famous Sauvignon Blanc.
L: Marlborough lies at the north-east tip of New Zealand's South Island, around the town of Blenheim. It's New Zealand's largest wine region by far, with about 30,000 hectares, around two-thirds of the country's vineyards. Its main valleys are the broad Wairau Valley and the smaller, higher Awatere Valley, separated by hills.
About two-thirds of New Zealand's vines

Marlborough is one of New Zealand's sunniest places, with long days and strong ultraviolet light, sheltered from westerly rain by mountains. Nights are cold, so the day and night range is wide. Grapes ripen slowly over a long season, keeping high acidity and intense aromas. Stony, free-draining alluvial soils from old riverbeds limit vigour. Spring frost is a risk.
What gives Marlborough wines both ripeness and high acidity?
A wide day and night range keeps acidity while sun ripens the fruit.

Commercial vines were first planted in Marlborough in 1973, by Montana, now Brancott Estate. In 1985, Cloudy Bay's first Sauvignon Blanc drew worldwide attention. From a few hundred hectares, the region grew to the largest in the country within 40 years, driven by export demand.
Marlborough is New Zealand's largest wine region.
Yes, with around two-thirds of the country's vineyards.
Marlborough sits at the top of the South Island, around Blenheim
Sunny days and cold nights give ripe fruit and high acidity
Planted from 1973, it grew fast after Cloudy Bay's 1985 success

Sauvignon Blanc covers about 80% of Marlborough's vineyards and most of New Zealand's wine exports. Marlborough Sauvignon is pungent and zesty: passion fruit, gooseberry, grapefruit, cut grass, green pepper and sometimes a sweaty, tropical edge, with very high acidity. It's almost always unoaked and bottled young.

Pinot Noir is the second grape, grown on clay-rich, cooler sites in the southern side valleys, like the Southern Valleys sub-region. It gives bright red cherry and spice, lighter than Central Otago's. Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Riesling and Gewürztraminer also grow, and Marlborough makes traditional method sparkling wine from Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.
Match each grape to its role.
Sauvignon leads by a long way.
Marlborough's Southern Valleys, with more clay, are where many of its best Pinot Noirs come from.
What share of Marlborough's vineyards is Sauvignon Blanc?
Sauvignon Blanc is about 80%, pungent and zesty
Pinot Noir is the second grape, from cooler clay sites
Chardonnay and sparkling wine add variety

Marlborough Sauvignon's tropical notes come from thiols, like 3MH and 3MHA, which smell of passion fruit and grapefruit; they're released during fermentation. Green notes, grass and green pepper, come from methoxypyrazines, kept by cool nights. Marlborough grapes have unusually high levels of both, which explains the intensity.

Machine harvesting at night breaks some skins, releasing thiol precursors; cool, protective fermentation in steel with selected yeasts keeps them. No oak and early bottling preserve freshness. Some producers make wild-yeast, barrel-fermented or lees-aged versions for texture, but the classic style is pure and pungent.
Which compounds give Marlborough Sauvignon its passion fruit aroma?

The Wairau Valley, broad and warmer, on stony and silty soils, gives the classic ripe, tropical style. The Awatere Valley, to the south-east, higher, drier, cooler and windier, gives more herbal, mineral, saline wines with tomato leaf and green notes. Many producers blend both for balance.
Which help create the Marlborough style?
Thiols give passion fruit; pyrazines give grass
Machine harvest and cool steel fermentation preserve aromas
Wairau is tropical; Awatere herbal and saline
Reading Marlborough and eating with it

Labels show the grape, Marlborough GI and vintage, with New Zealand's 85% rules for grape, region and vintage. Some name a sub-region, like Wairau Valley, Awatere Valley or Southern Valleys. Almost all bottles use screw caps; New Zealand led the switch from cork in the early 2000s. Appellation Marlborough Wine is a producer certification for quality and origin.

Marlborough Sauvignon suits green-lipped mussels, a local speciality, oysters, goat's cheese, salads, asparagus and Thai or Vietnamese food with herbs and lime. Pinot Noir suits salmon, duck and lamb. Serve Sauvignon at 7 to 9 degrees and drink within two years; Pinot at 14 to 16.
Which local shellfish suits Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc?
Marlborough is a major source of green-lipped mussels.
Drink Marlborough Sauvignon young. Its explosive aromas are at their best in the first year or two.
Most New Zealand wine is sealed with screw caps.
Yes. New Zealand led the move away from cork.
Labels show the GI and often a sub-region; screw caps are standard
Sauvignon suits green-lipped mussels, goat's cheese and herbs
Marlborough's map is simple and famous.
Classic Marlborough Sauvignon is aged in new oak.
Not true. It's usually unoaked to keep its aromas.
Which aromas are typical of Marlborough Sauvignon?
Vanilla and toast come from oak.
Commercial vines were first planted in Marlborough in ____.
Marlborough is sunny by day and cold at night
Sauvignon Blanc dominates, pungent and zesty
Thiols and pyrazines explain its intensity
It suits seafood, goat's cheese and herbs
